activities.caption: drag the divider — the machine and its mirror image
activities.name: tvMirrorCompare

config.prompt: Same 8 per cent, same five years, opposite directions — drag the divider:

before.label: Compounding — forward
before.text: 1,000 left invested at 8 per cent grows to 1,469 in five years: multiply by (1 + r) once per period of waiting.

after.label: Discounting — reverse
after.text: 1,469 arriving in five years is worth exactly 1,000 today at 8 per cent: divide by (1 + r) once per period of waiting.

config.why: Once any future cash flow can be converted into today's money, a bond, a factory, a mortgage and a startup all speak the same currency — which is what makes Net Present Value possible.

config.prompt: 10,000 is promised. Waiting shrinks what it is worth today — but how? Pick the curve discounting actually traces:
config.why: Discounting divides by (1 + r) per period: 10,000 in 5 years ≈ 6,806, in 10 ≈ 4,632 — and a million promised in forty years is only about 66,600 today at 7 per cent.

activities.caption: pin the doubling time on the Rule of 72
activities.name: tvRule72Place

config.prompt: Rule of 72: money doubles in roughly 72 ÷ r years. At 12 per cent, where does doubling land?
config.why: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 — at 6 per cent it is about 12 years, at 9 per cent about 8. The rule trades the exact logarithm for arithmetic you can do in your head.

activities.caption: call the total before the schedule does
activities.name: tvMortgageEstimate

config.prompt: You borrow 200,000 at 6 per cent over 25 years, paying the equal annual amount. Roughly what do you repay in total?
config.why: The equal payment works out near 15,600 a year (about 1,300 a month), so 25 years costs roughly 391,000 on a 200,000 loan — nothing hidden, that is simply what time costs at 6 per cent.

activities.caption: file each project: buy or walk away
activities.name: tvVerdictSort

config.prompt: You are the capital budget. File each candidate:

items.label: machine priced 6,000, paying 800 a year for 5 years at 8 per cent — PV of inflows ≈ 3,194
the same machine at a cut price — NPV turns +194
simple payback of 7.5 years against a 5-year life
a project measured as +1,000 of purchasing power right now

config.why: Accept if NPV is greater than zero: the test already accounts for the time value of money, the risk of the flows, and every alternative use of the capital — negative means wealth destroyed slowly enough that only bad accounting hides it.

activities.caption: set the hurdle — then live with it
activities.name: tvHurdleBranch

config.root: You are setting the corporate hurdle — the blended cost the company pays its lenders and shareholders.

start.text: Which way do you set it?

choices.label: Too high
choices.feedback: The firm starves itself of good investments — excessively high hurdles were a documented behaviour of cash-rich firms in the 2010s.

choices.label: Too low
choices.feedback: It invests in everything, including the projects that quietly destroy value.

high.text: Every bid is now measured against a bar almost nothing clears.

low.text: The queue of approved projects now includes the ones that quietly destroy value.

config.why: The rate carries the whole judgement: pure time value plus a risk premium — a promised dollar with a 50 per cent chance of never arriving must be valued as half a dollar, and scenario-weighted flows (25/60/15 across 1,200/800/300) enter as 765, not the cheerful 800.

activities.caption: pair each tool with its blind spot
activities.name: tvToolsMatch

config.prompt: Three tools compete with NPV — pair each with what trips it:

pairs.right: flows change sign more than once (a mine's cleanup bill) — two answers or none, and the number stops meaning anything
ignores everything after the recovery point and all of the time value before it

pairs.left: IRR between two projects of different sizes
pairs.right: can crown the small high-percentage project that creates less actual wealth
counts wealth created, in today's money — always the tiebreaker

config.why: Real organisations typically screen with payback, rank with IRR, and decide with NPV — managers love "this project returns 14 per cent", and it usually agrees.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — decomposing a 6 per cent rate
activities.name: tvDecompSpot

config.prompt: One line of this rate-decomposition note is wrong — click it:
lines: A 6 per cent lending rate decomposes into roughly 2 per cent expected inflation, 2 per cent real return, 2 per cent risk and liquidity premium.
A riskless real project in a zero-inflation world still demands a positive rate — capital has opportunity cost.
The discount rate is simply inflation, so a zero-inflation world would need a zero rate.
Discounting at inflation while ignoring risk overvalues every uncertain project on the desk.
Discounting asks: what else could this money do, and how sure am I of getting paid?
config.correction: The rate is never just inflation — it bundles pure time value, real return and a premium for uncertainty.
config.why: Discounting asks the broader comparison against what the money could earn elsewhere; a zero-inflation world still prices the waiting and the risk.
